knowledgeAnswers.rationale: An index of 1.50 means the month usually runs about half as much again as an average month. Option 1 confuses the index with a job count, and option 2 reverses the direction.

Adjusting for the season first stops predictable highs and lows from distorting the level of work. Option 2 removes the step the method depends on, and option 3 is untrue; a moving average can use any number of months.
The forecast is the underlying level multiplied by the month's index: 60 multiplied by 1.50 equals 90 jobs. Option 1 divides instead of multiplying, and option 3 leaves out the seasonal index.

practicalCriteria: Given at least two years of monthly job counts (the learner's own or a supplied practice set), the learner calculates a seasonal index for each month with the working shown.
The learner produces an adjusted three-month level and a forecast for the next month, with each step recorded and the result checked against the average month.
The learner compares a past forecast with the actual count, states the gap in jobs and states whether the underlying level needs updating.
passRule: 80% on knowledge checks; practical sign-off separate
evidenceRequired: Index table listing the months, years used, monthly averages and seasonal indices
Forecast log with the forecast date, forecast, actual count and gap
Written note on whether the underlying level is rising, falling or steady
Assessor observation of the learner explaining the forecast calculation
stopWorkCriteria: Stop and do not use a forecast to commit staff rosters or customer bookings until the indices have been checked against at least two years of records.
Stop if the seasonal pattern being used comes from another region or trade and has not been checked against the business's own records.
